newsitem.title: USA: Singer Laura Nyro, 49, dies of cancer.
newsitem.headline: Singer Laura Nyro, 49, dies of cancer.

text.p: Singer-songwriter Laura Nyro, who wrote many hit songs made famous by other performers, has died of ovarian cancer, her agent said on Wednesday.

Nyro, 49, who wrote top songs for Frank Sinatra, Barbra Streisand, the Fifth Dimension, Three Dog Night and Blood, Sweat & Tears, died on Tuesday at her home in Danbury, Connecticut, according to a brief statement by the Elizabeth Rush Agency in Weston, Massachusetts.
The statement said Nyro died "with the support and love of her son, Gil Bianchini, and her life's partner, Maria Desiderio..."
It said a private funeral service would be held but gave no details.
Nyro was born in New York City on Oct. 18, 1947.
Many critics agreed that Nyro, who blended catchy pop hooks with a cosmic soulfulness, was shamefully overlooked as a solo artist, especially during her creative heyday from 1966 to 1972.
Columbia Legacy in February released the first comprehensive collection of her work, the double-compact disc "Stoned Soul Picnic: The Best of Laura Nyro."
The 34 songs spanned the years 1966 to 1993, and featured guest appearances by Patti Labelle, Todd Rundgren, Randy Brecker, Alice Coltrane and Duane Allman.

The collection -- including her best-known tunes "And When I Die," "Eli's Comin'," "Save the Country," and "Stoney End," many of which were made famous by other artists -- received glowing reviews and sparked a new round of interest in her career, a Columbia Legacy spokesman said.

The daughter of a jazz trumpeter and a graduate of New York's High School of Music and Art, Nyro made a critical splash with her 1968 album "Eli and the Thirteenth Confession," released when she was only 20.
Her later albums fused jazz, world music and lyrics informed by a sort of ecological feminism.
In an interview published in the March issue of the British music magazine "Mojo," Nyro said she never set out to write hit records.
"That just happened," she said. "My artistry is not about hits for myself. It's about many years of learning about songwriting, moving some energy in music, learning the art of singing."
She said she always viewed the music business as a capitalist industry that thrived on formula.
"After that first album, I knew I had to fight for my freedom, and grow in a creative, poetic way rather than using a formula," Nyro said.

She also was one of the first major acts managed by recording industry mogul David Geffen, who was instrumental in getting her signed to Columbia Records, said Roy Hamm, a spokesman for Geffen Records in Los Angeles.
"It's safe to say they were close friends," Hamm said, adding Geffen's management of Nyro marked a turning point in Geffen's own career.
No statement was available from Geffen himself on Nyro's death, Hamm said.
